extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media industry observers, and readers concerned about AI in journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating a publisher's practices around AI-generated content, author attribution, and third-party licensing — including ethics, transparency, quality control, and monetization disclosures. Useful for assessing whether published pieces meet journalistic standards when AI or contractors are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author authenticity / real identity for bylines
rubrics_metrics.description: There was nothing in Drew Ortiz’s author biography at Sports Illustrated to suggest that he was anything other than human ... Outside of Sports Illustrated, Drew Ortiz doesn’t seem to exist. He has no social media presence and no publishing history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bylines should correspond to real, verifiable individuals. Avoid inventing personas, fake biographies, or using purchasable AI-generated headshots to create the illusion of real authors. Bylines serve to give credit and let readers hold writers accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of AI use and nonhuman authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: None of the articles credited to Ortiz or the other names contained any disclosure about the use of AI or that the writer wasn’t real, though they did eventually gain a disclaimer explaining that the content was 'created by a 3rd party.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should clearly disclose when content is AI-generated or produced by nontraditional/non-staff sources, and specifically state whether editorial staff were involved in creation or editing. Lack of disclosure is an ethical failure and erodes trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial oversight and staff involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Sports Illustrated editorial staff are not involved in the creation of this content' (disclaimer cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content published under a media brand should have appropriate editorial oversight: fact-checking, editing, and accountability by the publication’s editorial staff. If editorial staff are not involved, that must be disclosed and the lack of oversight treated as a risk factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of writing: coherence, clarity, grammar, and formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: The AI authors’ writing often sounds like it was written by an alien; ... bizarre-sounding language and glaring formatting discrepancies. Example: a five-point list where each number is just number one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Published pieces must meet basic standards of readability and formatting (coherent prose, correct numbering, sensible syntax). Poorly constructed or garbled language is a signal of inadequate editing and should not be published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual accuracy and avoidance of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: We caught CNET and Bankrate ... publishing barely-disclosed AI content that was filled with factual mistakes and even plagiarism; in the ensuing storm of criticism, CNET issued corrections to more than half its AI-generated articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and contractors must fact-check content and run plagiarism checks. When factual errors or plagiarism are found, issue corrections promptly and transparently. Use counter-plagiarism tools as part of editorial workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and explanation when bylines/posts are reattributed or removed
rubrics_metrics.description: Each time an author was switched out, the posts they supposedly penned would be reattributed to the new persona, with no editor’s note explaining the change in byline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When bylines are changed or content is reattributed, include an editor’s note describing why the change occurred and preserve a record of original attribution. Silent reattribution is misleading to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vetting, monitoring, and accountability for third-party vendors/contractors
rubrics_metrics.description: According to our initial investigation, this is not accurate. The articles in question were product reviews and were licensed content from an external, third-party company, AdVon Commerce. ... We continually monitor our partners and were in the midst of a review when these allegations were raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers must vet third-party content providers, monitor partnerships continuously, require transparency about authorship, and act (remove content/terminate partnerships) when standards are violated. Taking vendors at their word without verification is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mass-producing low-quality AI content; prioritize quality over quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s not about 'crank out AI content and do as much as you can,' ... 'more isn't better; better is better.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not deploy generative AI to churn out large volumes of low-quality, monetized content. Prioritize editorial quality and accuracy; automated scale without quality controls harms reputation and can lead to search-engine penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of monetization and affiliate relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Phony writers ... used to pump out AI-generated buying guides that are monetized by affiliate links that provide a financial kickback when readers click them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When content is monetized via affiliate links or commercial partnerships, disclose those relationships clearly to readers. Commercial incentives should not be concealed behind fake bylines or undisclosed third-party content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AI-detection and counter-AI tools as part of content policy
rubrics_metrics.description: AdVon has assured us that all of the articles in question were written and edited by humans. According to AdVon, their writers, editors, and researchers create and curate content and follow a policy that involves using both counter-plagiarism and counter-AI software on all content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ counter-AI detection tools alongside plagiarism detection in editorial workflows if publishers accept third-party or AI-assisted content. Be transparent about such measures and verify their effective use rather than relying on vendor claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely corrections, removals, and public accountability for errors
rubrics_metrics.description: When The Arena Group first started publishing AI-generated health advice ... its first story was riddled with errors, prompting it to issue a massive correction. CNET issued corrections to more than half its AI-generated articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When problematic content is identified (errors, misleading authorship, plagiarism), promptly issue corrections or remove content and explain the action to readers. Public accountability helps restore trust.
